chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked about chess, and about the game of youths which is called the game of the Emir, and about the game of the three, so he said:
He said: 'Do you see, if the truth were differentiated from the falsehood, with which of these two would it be?' I said: 'With the falsehood.' He said: 'Therefore, there is no goodness in it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on chess in Shia Islam according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) evaluates chess (*al-shatranj*) and similar games like *Lu'bat al-Amir* through a logical test of alignment with truth. He posits that if these games were distinct from falsehood, they would naturally align with falsehood, thereby lacking inherent goodness (*la khayra fih*). This reasoning underscores the Shia scholarly view that such games distract from spiritual clarity and are often categorized as *makruh* (disliked) or *haram* (prohibited) due to their association with idle amusement that diverts the heart from divine remembrance.
